results.title: Pre-analytical phase errors constitute the vast majority of ... - PubMed
results.content: Go to  My NCBI account settings  to confirm your email and then refresh this page. # Pre-analytical phase errors constitute the vast majority of errors in clinical laboratory testing. # Pre-analytical phase errors constitute the vast majority of errors in clinical laboratory testing. **Objectives:**  Clinical laboratory errors pose a threat to patient safety and previous studies have demonstrated that pre-analytical error is the most common error type. Errors were adjudicated and binned into pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical phases. Among these errors, 85,894 (98.4 %, 984,000 ppm) were in the pre-analytical, 451 (0.5 %, 5,000 ppm) were in the analytical, and 972 (1.1 %, 11,000 ppm) occurred in the post-analytical phase. When excluding hemolysis, there were 26,569 errors documented (0.06 %, 600 ppm of billable results), among which 94.6 %, 1.7 % (17,000 ppm) and 3.7 % (37,000 ppm) were in the pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical phase respectively. **Keywords:**  error rate; hemolysis; laboratory error; pre-analytical error; specimen integrity.

results.title: A retrospective analysis of 400 publications reveals patterns ... - eLife
results.content: Notably, 47 authors (16.3%, 95% CI: 11.4–19.6%) published at least one non-reproducible claim, with one author reaching up to 83% irreproducibility (5 challenged claims out of 6 from two articles). Our studies point to a significant role of experience: PIs that had previously worked in another *Drosophil*a immunity laboratory to the extent that they published a first author article in that laboratory were less prone to publish irreproducible claims. We observed that authors with a more exploratory research style have slightly higher proportions of challenged claims and a significantly higher proportion of unchallenged claims, the latter being more likely to be challenged as shown by our experimental replication. These include i) articles being published by authors working in top-ranked institutions, ii) articles being published in trophy journals, iii) the absence of follow-up studies (i.e. being ‘unchallenged’), and iv) articles being published by authors with an exploratory research style.In contrast, having published as first author in another laboratory within the field, and publishing in high-impact journals but not trophy journals correlate with higher reproducibility.
